title: Tree canopy grants, parking rates and homelessness advocacy
subtitle: Climate adaptation grant, health and safety policies, culture committee terms of reference, and a closed session on a labour matter.
overview: Council approved two federal grant applications to the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. The first is Trees for Waterloo, with a City contribution of up to $1,900,000, including $1,007,000 from the Climate Action Reserve Fund. The second would upgrade back-up electric power at Fire Station 3, Parkview Cemetery, RIM Park and the Waterloo Service Centre, with a City contribution of up to $400,000. Both passed {{vote:m3}} {{vote:m4}}.

Council approved 2025 parking increases: 3.5% for monthly permits and $0.25 for hourly rates, with forecasts for 2026-2034 approved in principle {{vote:m6}}. Staff said rates had not risen for three years. Council also backed the Solve the Crisis campaign, which asks the province and federal government to act on homelessness, mental health and addictions {{vote:m7}}.

Council also approved updated health and safety, respectful workplace and workplace violence policies {{vote:m2}}, and revised terms of reference for the Advisory Committee on Culture, changing "cultural industries" to "creative industries" {{vote:m5}}. Council met in closed session on a labour matter involving the firefighters' association. The minutes record no public report from it.

decisions.detail: Council approved the grant application to the Federation of Canadian Municipalities and a City contribution of up to $1,900,000, including $1,007,000 from the Climate Action Reserve Fund {{vote:m3}}.
Council approved a grant application to upgrade back-up power at Fire Station 3, Parkview Cemetery, RIM Park and the Waterloo Service Centre, with a City contribution of up to $400,000 {{vote:m4}}.
Council approved a 3.5% monthly permit increase and a $0.25 hourly rate increase for 2025, and approved the 2026-2034 forecasts in principle {{vote:m6}}.
Council supported the campaign and called on the province and federal government to act, including naming a responsible minister and creating a provincial task force {{vote:m7}}.

Council approved the Health and Safety Policy Statement, the Respectful Workplace Policy and Program, and the Workplace Violence Policy and Program, and received the 2023 annual report summary {{vote:m2}}.

decisions.item: Advisory Committee on Culture terms of reference
decisions.detail: Council approved revised terms of reference, changing "cultural industries" to "creative industries" in the skills section {{vote:m5}}.

debate: On the culture committee, one councillor welcomed adding creative industries but worried that heritage and culture could be lost, and asked how equity and inclusion would be built into the work. Staff said artist voices are not well represented now, many local artists belong to equity-deserving groups, and recruitment would support diversity.
On health and safety policies, the Mayor asked how the City's equity team had shaped them. Staff said the team's feedback led to expanded definitions, clearer sections and plainer language.

On parking rates, a councillor asked about affordability. Staff said increases are modelled every three years at roughly 2% a year, which is below what the model would allow. Staff said demand is highest near King Street and Willis Way.
On bike lockers, councillors noted a waiting list with little turnover. Staff said more lockers are on order and the program is subsidized, with the City covering a large share of its cost.

In presenting the Solve the Crisis motion, the Mayor said property taxes were not designed for health and housing problems, that over a dozen provincial ministries are involved with no single lead, and that provincial and federal funding is often short-term. Another councillor supported a single point of contact.
